one_liner: Official Rust/C implementation of BLAKE3, a Merkle-tree hash/XOF/MAC about 4x faster than SHA-256 on long single-core inputs.
what_it_does: Implements the BLAKE3 hash function, which covers what SHA-256/SHA3-256 do (a collision-resistant 256-bit digest) and adds keyed-MAC, key-derivation and extendable, seekable-output modes in one algorithm with no variants. The Rust crate offers blake3::hash(), an incremental Hasher (update/finalize/finalize_xof), keyed_hash and derive_key; the C library offers blake3_hasher_init/update/finalize with the same modes, and b3sum is a sha256sum-style CLI. The digests differ from SHA-2/SHA-3/BLAKE2, so it can replace those only where you control both the side that computes the hash and the side that checks it.
how_it_is_fast: The input is cut into 1 KiB chunks that form the leaves of a binary Merkle tree (derived from the Bao tree mode), so chunks are independent and the SIMD code compresses 4, 8 or 16 of them at once, one 32-bit word per vector lane (SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX-512). This 'word-based' parallelism is why throughput jumps between 2 and 16 KiB. The compression function is BLAKE2s's 32-bit ARX core, with rounds cut from 10 to 7 and a message schedule simplified to one repeated permutation. On x86-64, runtime CPU detection selects hand-written assembly, and optional Rayon (Rust) or oneTBB (C) spreads subtrees across cores.
when_to_use: Content addressing, deduplication, build caches and file-integrity checks on inputs of several KiB or more, where you choose the hash (the README lists Cargo, ccache, Bazel, Nix, LLVM and OpenZFS as adopters).
x86-64 hosts with AVX2 or AVX-512: on eBASH, single-thread long-message cost is 0.51-0.60 cycles/byte, against 2.02-2.21 for SHA-NI SHA-256 and 5.5-6.5 for SHA3-256.

Hashing large in-memory buffers or files on many cores: update_rayon, update_mmap_rayon and blake3_hasher_update_tbb split the tree across threads, and the spec shows near-linear scaling up to 16 threads.
When you need a MAC, a KDF or arbitrary-length/seekable output and would otherwise layer HMAC/HKDF/SHAKE on a plain hash.
Verified streaming or incremental verification of large blobs through the tree structure (the Bao project).
when_not_to_use: Formats or protocols that mandate SHA-256/SHA-3 (FIPS-validated modules, TLS, X.509, existing on-disk or wire formats): the digest is not compatible.

Short and medium messages on CPUs with SHA-256 instructions. eBASH shows SHA-256 ahead at 576 and 1536 bytes on Tiger Lake (2.34 vs 2.88 cycles/byte at 1536 B) and on Zen 4 (2.10 vs 3.76), and issue #315 reports single-thread b3sum slower than `openssl sha256` on Apple Silicon.
Password storage or deriving keys from passwords: the README says to use Argon2 instead.
Low-end cores without wide SIMD: here BLAKE3 performs like BLAKE2s (spec Figure 5, ARM1176), and issue #403 reports the NEON build slower than the portable one on a Cortex-A9.
Multithreaded hashing of small inputs or of big files on spinning disks: update_rayon is slower than update below about 128 KiB on x86-64, and parallel mmap reads thrash HDDs (issue #31).

integration.form: crate (blake3, plus the b3sum CLI crate) and a C static/shared library, built with CMake or by compiling the .c/.S files directly
integration.dependencies: Rust: arrayvec, constant_time_eq, cfg-if, cpufeatures (x86 only). Optional: rayon-core, memmap2, digest, serde, zeroize. Build dependency: cc. C: none, with optional oneTBB for multithreading.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 (edition 2024; CI builds on 1.85.1, but there is no formal MSRV policy). C: GCC, Clang or MSVC (tested in CI), CMake 3.9+. The TBB path needs a C++20 compiler and -fno-exceptions.
integration.platforms: x86 and x86-64 (SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX-512, runtime dispatch, assembly for Unix, Windows MSVC and Windows GNU). AArch64 NEON is on by default. ARMv7 NEON and WASM SIMD are compile-time opt-ins. Other targets use the portable fallback, and CI covers big-endian powerpc64 and s390x.
integration.thread_safety: A Hasher/blake3_hasher is a plain value with no shared state, so use one per thread or clone it. Only update_rayon/update_mmap_rayon (Rust) and blake3_hasher_update_tbb (C) are multithreaded internally; all other APIs are single-threaded. The C CPU-feature cache uses atomics when stdatomic.h is available and Interlocked calls on MSVC.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the API shape (init/update/finalize) matches a SHA-256 streaming hasher, but the output values differ, so existing stored or exchanged digests cannot be checked. RustCrypto digest traits exist only behind the traits-preview feature, which has no SemVer guarantee.

gotchas: The widely quoted 10-20x-over-SHA-256 figures come from multithreaded mmap hashing (b3sum's default) or from a 2019 Cascade Lake CPU without SHA-NI. The single-thread lead over hardware SHA-256 is about 3.4-4.3x at long lengths and turns into a loss around 0.5-1.5 KiB.

sizeof(blake3_hasher) is 1912 bytes on x86-64 because it holds a 55-entry chaining-value stack. That is large for per-object or on-stack state, and the C library does not implement the spec's reduced-maximum-length option.

The Rust build compiles C/assembly through cc. If no suitable C compiler (or no AVX-512-capable one) is found, it quietly falls back to a slower pure-Rust build. NEON on non-AArch64 targets and WASM SIMD are not runtime-detected: enabling them produces binaries that assume the feature.

Outputs shorter than 32 bytes give proportionally less security, and the XOF seek offset should not be treated as secret. Compare Hash values with the type's constant-time == rather than as byte slices.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick BLAKE3 over sha256-simd, Intel ISA-L multi-buffer SHA, j-lanes or S-HASH when you are free to change the digest: those keep SHA-256 compatibility or need many independent buffers, while BLAKE3 parallelizes a single message. Pick it over KangarooTwelve (XKCP) for peak speed at shorter lengths (1 KiB vs 8 KiB leaves), built-in multithreading and keyed/KDF modes; pick K12 when you want a Keccak/SHA-3-family primitive.
verified_claims_summary: On eBASH (SUPERCOP 20260831; single-core 'long message' = cycle difference between 18208- and 1824-byte inputs), the BLAKE3 avx512 build (Clang 14, -O3) on an Intel Core i7-1165G7 (Tiger Lake, AVX-512 + SHA-NI) takes a median 0.51 cycles/byte versus 2.21 for the fastest SHA-256 implementation, 5.50 for SHA3-256 and 2.99 for BLAKE2b (about 4.3x, 10.8x, 5.9x), and a Ryzen 7 7700 gives 0.60 vs 2.02 for SHA-256. The project's own 2020 chart (16 KiB, one thread, Xeon 8275CL without SHA-NI, OpenSSL 1.1.1d) shows about 14x over SHA-256, a gap that does not carry over to CPUs with SHA instructions.
status_note: Actively maintained (v1.8.7 released 2026-08-20, commits through 2026-09-10, about 189M crates.io downloads) and licensed CC0 or Apache-2.0 (with or without the LLVM exception), so the C files can be vendored into any build.
